tip: Past-tense 'I' verbs end in -ais, and the i pronoun follows: ddwedais i means I said.
Soft mutation can delete g entirely. gorsaf becomes orsaf after o'r, giving o'r orsaf (from the station).
The linking yn soft-mutates the word after it, so mantais turns into fantais in yn fantais.
The object of an inflected verb soft-mutates its first word: dwy becomes ddwy in Prynais i ddwy gôt.
To negate a definite object, Welsh uses mo plus a pronoun ending. mo + hi becomes mohoni (not her).
dysgu covers both learning and teaching. Here Dysgais i nofio means I learned to swim.
The 'that' in a reported clause is bod, softened to fod here: Sylwais i fod y drws ar agor.
Starting with a time word like Ddoe doesn't change the verb, prynais i still carries the -ais ending for I bought.
'I was born' is literally 'I got my birth': Cefais i fy ngeni, using cael plus fy plus the verb.
Negative past uses aspirate mutation plus ddim: clywais becomes Chlywais i ddim (I didn't hear).
South Welsh shows possession with gyda: Doedd dim amser gyda fi means I had no time.
cwrdd takes the linker â for the person you meet: Cwrddais i â ffrind (I met a friend).
The object of an inflected verb soft-mutates its first word: dysgu becomes ddysgu after Dechreuais i (I started).
After o (from), soft mutation turns Ll into L: Lloegr becomes Loegr in o Loegr.
The ending -ûm is a literary 'I' past. Cyfarfûm i (I met) is more formal than spoken cwrddais i.
Adjectives follow the noun in Welsh: cawl blasus is literally soup tasty for tasty soup.
A verb-noun can act as the subject, like a gerund: parcio means 'parking' in Mae parcio'n anodd.
Ga i...? asks 'may I' and soft-mutates the next verb: defnyddio becomes ddefnyddio.
mynd is irregular in the past: Est ti means you went, as in Est ti i'r parti (did you go to the party).
Putting the subject first with wnaeth marks emphasis: Owain wnaeth ffeindio means it was Owain who found.
After Rhaid i plus a person, the verb soft-mutates: cofio becomes gofio in Rhaid i mi gofio.
The -wn i ending is conditional 'would': Hoffwn i means I would like, gentler than saying I want.
The object 'me' wraps the verb as fy...i: fy helpu i means help me in Alli di fy helpu i.
arfer after Roedd means 'used to' for old habits: Roedd hi'n arfer byw is she used to live.
You thank 'to' someone in Welsh: diolch takes i, so Diolchodd hi i'r meddyg is she thanked the doctor.
'to her' contracts to iddi, and the verb soft-mutates: talu becomes dalu in Rhaid iddi hi dalu.
After Os (if), the present doi di covers the future: Os doi di'n gynnar means if you come early.
The imperfect Roedd e'n gweithio is the ongoing background, and the -ais past ffoniais i marks the one-off event.
Indirect yes/no questions use a for 'whether': Gofynnodd...a oeddwn i means asked if I was.
'I should have' is Dylwn i fod wedi plus a verb: Dylwn i fod wedi edrych means I should have looked.
Need is felt 'on' you in Welsh: angen...arna i means I need, so Roedd angen...arna i is I needed.
dod â, literally 'come with', means 'bring': Daeth e â blodau is he brought flowers.
'before I arrived' is cyn i fi plus a soft-mutated verb: cyrraedd becomes gyrraedd in cyn i fi gyrraedd.
Add -ach for 'more' and na for 'than': sych becomes sychach, and sychach na'r llynedd is drier than last year.
